title: Cross-service contract and schema evolution playbook
author: Ethan Liu
body:
Summary:
This playbook defines a pragmatic, enforceable process for defining, validating, evolving, and retiring cross-service JSON/HTTP contracts used across Redwood inference stacks (API gateways, routing proxies, runtime sidecars, and model-serving endpoints). It consolidates requirements from API standards, model-serving stability, and infra rollout constraints into a single reference engineers can follow to avoid breaking production dependencies.

Why this matters:
- Multiple services (frontend SDKs, edge proxies, routing layers, runtime backends) share contract expectations. Uncoordinated schema changes cause silent regressions, billing anomalies, and latency regressions.
- Model-serving contracts are particularly brittle: small output-schema changes can break downstream batching, caching, and metric extraction.
- A clear, automated evolution path reduces outage risk and speeds feature delivery.

Scope and applicability:
- Scope: JSON-based request/response schemas, streaming payload envelopes, header-level contract metadata, and client-server compatibility semantics.
- Applies to: all services under the Redwood inference surface (hosted API, Dedicated, Private runtime sidecars, and console integrations).
- Excludes: internal-only feature flags not exposed via APIs, and binary model artifact formats (handled by model-artifact-provenance).

Key terminology:
- Contract: signed expectation describing request/response shapes and semantics.
- Producer: service that emits the schema (e.g., model-serving runtime).
- Consumer: service that depends on the schema (e.g., aggregator, billing).
- Minor-compatible change: additive, non-breaking (new optional property).
- Major-incompatible change: removes/renames/changes semantics of fields.

Contract format (required fields):
- id: stable contract identifier (reverse-dns style), e.g. com.redwood.model.response.v1
- version: semver-like token: MAJOR.MINOR (we disallow patch-level; patch used for implementation only)
- description: single-sentence intent
- producer: service owner team
- schema: JSON Schema draft-07 compatible object (stringified in the contract manifest)
- compatibility: "backward" | "forward" | "none"
- lifecycle: draft | published | deprecated | retired

Example contract manifest (contract.json):
{
  "id": "com.redwood.runtime.model-output",
  "version": "1.2",
  "description": "Structured generation output for text-completion endpoints",
  "producer": "eng-serving-runtime",
  "compatibility": "backward",
  "lifecycle": "published",
  "schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "request_id": {"type": "string"},
      "tokens": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}},
      "score": {"type": "number"},
      "metadata": {"type": "object", "additionalProperties": true}
    },
    "required": ["request_id", "tokens"]
  }
}

Validation and CI gates:
1) Schema linting: all contract manifests must pass the contract-lint ruleset (see repo: infra/contract-lint).
   - Command (CI): ./tools/contract-lint --path contracts/ --require-ids
2) Consumer-driven tests: every consumer must publish a minimal fixture and acceptance test referencing contract id+version.
   - Example (pytest): tests/test_contract_compat.py asserts runtime output validates against contract schema.
3) Contract signing: when publishing MAJOR version bumps, producer must create a signed change note and an ADR referencing impact assessment. CI will block merging until signoff.
4) Canary validation: new MAJOR versions require a 7-day canary with traffic-scoped routes (see rollout steps).

Backward/forward compatibility rules (short checklist):
- Additive fields: allowed if marked optional in schema and documented.
- Field renames: forbidden without a MAJOR bump and migration plan.
- Type changes: forbidden (MAJOR required).
- Moving nested fields: requires compatibility proof and consumer test adjustments.
- Header-level contract hints (x-contract-version) must be included on cross-cluster calls.

Rollout and migration procedure (step-by-step):
1) Design: Producer drafts new contract manifest and a brief compatibility assessment (1–2 pages). Attach to PR.
2) Consumer discovery: run static graph analysis to list consumers (command: ./tools/contract-graph --id com.redwood.runtime.model-output).
3) Consumer opt-in tests: each consumer adds an opt-in test fixture for new version and runs smoke tests in staging.
4) Canary publish: producer publishes new version to canary deployment namespace. Expose via a canary header: "x-contract-canary: <version>".
5) Monitoring window (7 days): monitor SLI deltas (errors, invalid-schema, p50/p95 latency) and business metrics (cost per token, billing noise). Use Redwood Console prehook dashboard: /dashboards/contract-canary.
6) Gradual ramp: if no regressions, increase traffic 5x per day until 100%. If regressions are detected, automatically revert with the canary rollback job.
7) Publish: mark lifecycle=published and update contract index. Notify consumer teams via email/Slack with migration checklist.

SLOs and telemetry (what to monitor):
- Contract validation failures: target < 0.01% of requests after 24h of GA.
- Schema-invalid responses (downstream): alert if > 0.05% sustained for 30m.
- Latency delta attributable to contract change: p95 increase <= 15% or require rollback.
Telemetry to emit (producer):
- contract.id, contract.version, validation.status (ok|invalid), validation.reason, request_id, route
- consumer-side metric: contract.validate.success ratio and consumer.fallback.count

Ownership, exceptions, and decision gates:
- Contract steward: the producer service owner is the primary steward and approver for minor changes.
- Cross-team major changes require: (a) owner-team signoff; (b) consumer-team acknowledgement; (c) infra SRE review; (d) product-impact assessment.
- Exceptions: short-lived experimental fields are allowed under lifecycle=draft and must include an explicit TTL and owner. Experimental contracts must not be used by production consumers without a feature-flagged opt-in.

Compatibility matrix (example):
| Contract id | Current version | Consumers (team) | Allowed change class | Notes |
| com.redwood.runtime.model-output | 1.2 | console-ingest (eng-platform), billing (finance), deduper (eng-serving-runtime) | minor-additions | avoid adding top-level new property named "tokens" |

Operational playbook for incident response to contract breakages:
1) Pager alert triggers: "contract.validation.rate" fires.
2) Run: ./tools/contract-inspect --id <contract> --since 10m to enumerate failing payloads.
3) If root cause is producer: rollback to previous contract implementation and/or toggle compatibility shim in gateway.
4) If root cause is consumer: implement graceful fallback, update consumer parsing, and request staged deploy.
5) Postmortem: update contract manifest with discovered gaps and record remediation steps in regression-triage.

Appendix A — Minimal CI YAML (example):
name: Contract CI
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - run: ./tools/contract-lint --path contracts/
  consumer-tests:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - run: pytest tests/ --contract-id ${{ inputs.contract_id }}

Appendix B — Small compatibility checklist for reviewers:
- Is the change additive? If yes, mark minor.
- Are all consumers discovered and fixture-tested?
- Are telemetry keys present?
- Is there a fallback path for invalid payloads?
- Is the rollout plan and SLA window specified?

Related pages and references:
